newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian policeman killed in tense southern town.
newsitem.headline: Albanian policeman killed in tense southern town.

text.p: An Albanian policeman was shot dead on Wednesday in the tense southern port town of Vlore, where three people died this week in anti-government protests.
An Interior Ministry statement said the policeman was shot dead by automatic gunfire near his home in the Adriatic town, scene of clashes between riot police and protesters on Monday and Tuesday.
It identified the policeman as Shezai Zani, 30. Reporters in Vlore said a car had sped through the town during the day with someone firing an automatic rifle from the window.
Vlore police chief Ethem Kurti told Reuters Zani was in charge of guarding "places of special importance" and had not taken part in the clashes earlier this week.
An anti-government protester was shot dead and two others died of heart attacks during the clashes in which about 150 people were injured.
Earlier on Wednesday, thousands of protesters staged an eighth day of demonstrations in Vlore, enraged by the collapse of several dubious investment schemes.

More than 5,000 disillusioned investors cheered opposition leaders who told the crowd they had teamed up with trade unions to form a cross-party political alliance, demanding the ouster of the right-wing government of President Sali Berisha.
The Adriatic port town has been the scene of some of the worst unrest Albania has seen since communism was toppled in 1990.
Protests were sparked by the collapse of a local pyramid investment scheme in which large parts of the population had sunk their life savings, leaving them destitute.

Truckloads of riot police prevented opposition parties from staging a rally in Tirana, some 150 km (90 miles) to the north, in a repeat of last weekend's events when police broke up an anti-government gathering in capital's main Skanderbeg Square.
Other demonstrations took place in four towns near the Greek border, but there were no reports of violence.

Opposition leaders say the ruling Democrats have stood idle while pyramid schemes sprang up across the mountainous country over the past six years. They allege the party has used the funds to finance its re-election campaign last year.
Democratic Party leaders vowed to get tough on the protesters, which they have denounced as a bunch of left-wing extremists trying to destabilise the troubled Balkan nation.
There was strong international criticism on Wednesday of the Albanian government's handling of the crisis.

The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe said it was deeply worried about the violence, warning that the potential for a serious crisis was at hand. Britain said it was appalled by the violence, expressing concern about reports of arrests and intimidation of opposition leaders.
Albania's exiled King Leka predicted the wave of civil unrest would force Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi's resignation within 24 hours, and said he was ready to step in.
"All the reports that I am getting from Albania at this moment are that the only person they have any interest in is myself," Leka told Reuters at his home in South Africa.
"We expect Prime Minister Meksi to resign sometime today or tomorrow. All the parties with the exception of the Democratic Party are now demanding a referendum."

But Democratic Party chief and Foreign Minister Tritan Shehu, seen as a confidant of Berisha, insisted the government had no plans to resign. Asked whether any cabinet changes were afoot, he told Reuters: "Absolutely not."
